messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 74
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Welder
- Trauma Type: Civilian in war zone
- Pcl5: 60

He is a 74-year-old South Eastern Asian man who has spent most of his adult life working as a welder, a trade that he describes with quiet pride because it allowed him to build things with his hands and provide for his family. When he talks about his life now, he moves back and forth between the present and the war years as if the past is never far from the surface. He is married and still lives with his wife, though he often says that in some ways he feels like he has been “gone” from himself for many years.

He grew up in a city that later became a place of shells, checkpoints, and sudden fear. Before the war, he remembers ordinary sounds: vendors calling in the street, children playing, the steady rhythm of work. When the fighting reached his neighborhood, those sounds were replaced by explosions, shouting, and the metallic slam of doors being locked in a rush. He was a civilian then, trying to keep his family alive while moving through a city that no longer felt like home. He describes the war as a time of constant calculation—how much water was left, which road might still be open, whether the next loud noise was far away or already close. He learned to read danger quickly, to stay low, and to make decisions before fear could overtake him.

He speaks most vividly about one event in particular, though he never tells it in a straight line. One day, while trying to get home, he was caught in an attack that struck near civilians sheltering in the street. He remembers smoke, dust, and the sensation that the world had split open. He does not dwell on graphic detail, but his face changes when he says that after that day he could no longer assume that safety meant anything. He lost neighbors. He spent hours searching for relatives and helping carry injured people where he could. The memory feels less like a story than a permanent injury. Even now, he says that when he closes his eyes, he can still hear the sharp crack of gunfire and the low, rising sounds of people crying out.

After surviving the war, he eventually left and rebuilt his life, including his work as a welder. The steady heat of the torch and the focus required by metalwork gave him a kind of structure he had not had for years. Yet even in the workshop he remains alert in ways others do not understand. Loud bangs from dropped tools or the sudden hiss of steam make him jump before he can stop himself. He turns his head automatically when he hears tires squeal, and if someone walks up behind him unexpectedly, he reacts as if bracing for impact. He keeps track of exits wherever he goes. In public places, he prefers to sit facing the door, and he becomes noticeably tense when he cannot see what is happening around him.

His sleep has been poor for a long time. He falls asleep exhausted, but he wakes often, sometimes drenched in sweat after dreaming of running through smoke or being trapped while sirens sound in the distance. On some nights he does not remember the dream clearly, only the feeling of panic that lingers after waking. He rises early and sits quietly with tea, trying to steady himself before the day begins. During the day he can be drawn back into the war by the smallest reminder—a smell of burning metal, the pop of fireworks, the sight of a soldier in uniform on television. When this happens, he becomes distant and preoccupied, as if he is no longer fully with the people around him. His wife notices that he grows irritable without warning, then ashamed of himself for it. He says he does not like how easily anger comes now, especially toward the family he has spent his life trying to protect.

He also carries a heavy sense of guilt. He speaks about those who did not survive and about moments when he had to choose between speed and helping more people. He wonders whether he should have done more, though when he says this it is clear that he has carried the question for decades without finding an answer. He avoids war-related news and does not like gatherings where people talk too freely about conflict, because it leaves him feeling cornered by memory. At the same time, he does not want to be seen as weak, so he minimizes his distress and keeps much of it private. Over the course of several sessions, it becomes clear that he has organized his life around endurance. He works, he helps around the house, he attends to his grandchildren when he can, but all of it happens alongside a constant internal vigilance, as though some part of him is still in the war zone, waiting for the next sound that means he must run.
